lessons.lessonTitle: Lesson 1: CSS Syntax, Rules, and Element/Class/ID Selectors

questions.question: Which of the following correctly describes the 4-part specificity weight calculation for standard CSS selectors (Inline, ID, Class/Attribute/Pseudo-class, Element/Pseudo-element)?
options: Universal selector * (1,0,0,0) > ID (0,1,0,0) > Class (0,0,1,0) > Element (0,0,0,1)
Inline styles (1,0,0,0) > ID (#id: 0,1,0,0) > Class/Attribute/Pseudo-class (.class, [attr], :hover: 0,0,1,0) > Element/Pseudo-element (div, ::after: 0,0,0,1)
ID (1,0,0,0) > Inline styles (0,1,0,0) > Element (0,0,1,0) > Class (0,0,0,1)
questions.explanation: CSS Specificity is calculated as a 4-tier vector (a, b, c, d): Inline styles = (1,0,0,0), ID selectors = (0,1,0,0), Classes/Attributes/Pseudo-classes = (0,0,1,0), and Elements/Pseudo-elements = (0,0,0,1).

questions.question: What is the specificity weight of the universal selector (`*`) in CSS?
options: 0,0,0,1 (Equivalent to a standard HTML tag name selector)
0,0,0,0 (Zero specificity, easily overridden by any element, class, or ID selector)
1,0,0,0 (Highest priority across all selectors)
0,1,0,0 (Equivalent to an ID selector)
questions.explanation: The universal selector (`*`) has a specificity value of (0,0,0,0); it matches every element but contributes zero specificity points to the calculation.

questions.question:
Which combinator selector matches only paragraphs (`

`) that are direct, immediate children of a `

` element?
options: div + p
div p
div > p
div ~ p
questions.explanation: The child combinator (`>`) targets direct children only, whereas the descendant combinator (space) targets all descendants regardless of nesting depth.

questions.question: What does the adjacent sibling combinator `h2 + p` select in an HTML document?
options:
A `

` element that is placed immediately after an `

` element sharing the exact same parent

Every `

` element that follows an `

` at any point within the same parent container

Both the `

` and `

` elements merged together into a single flexbox item

All `

` elements located anywhere inside the preceding `

` element
questions.explanation: The adjacent sibling combinator (`+`) matches an element only if it immediately follows the specified element and both share the same parent.

questions.question: Which attribute selector matches elements whose `href` attribute begins exactly with 'https://'?
options: a[href~="https://"]
a[href^="https://"]
a[href$="https://"]
a[href*="https://"]
questions.explanation: `^=` matches values that start with the specified string, `$=` matches values that end with the string, and `*=` matches substrings appearing anywhere.

questions.question: What is the difference between the pseudo-classes `:nth-child(2)` and `:nth-of-type(2)` when applied to `p:nth-child(2)` vs `p:nth-of-type(2)`?
options:
`p:nth-child(2)` selects the element only if it is the 2nd overall child of its parent and is a `

`, whereas `p:nth-of-type(2)` selects the 2nd `

` among all paragraph siblings regardless of other elements
`p:nth-of-type(2)` requires an explicit `class` attribute, whereas `:nth-child(2)` does not
`p:nth-child(2)` only counts even numbered elements, while `p:nth-of-type(2)` counts odd elements
There is no difference; modern CSS treats them as interchangeable aliases
questions.explanation: `:nth-child(n)` checks the element's index among all siblings regardless of tag type, while `:nth-of-type(n)` filters siblings by the specific element tag type first before indexing.

questions.question: Which property is strictly required when declaring pseudo-elements `::before` or `::after` for them to render on the page?
options: visibility
position
content
display
questions.explanation: Pseudo-elements `::before` and `::after` will not render in the document tree unless the `content` property is explicitly defined (even as an empty string `content: '';`).

questions.question: How does the pseudo-class `:is()` differ from `:where()` in modern CSS?
options: `:is()` adopts the specificity of its most specific argument in the selector list, whereas `:where()` always has zero specificity (0,0,0,0)
`:where()` only works on desktop browsers, while `:is()` is mobile-only
`:is()` is strictly case-sensitive, whereas `:where()` ignores letter casing
`:where()` can only contain element selectors, while `:is()` can only contain IDs
questions.explanation: Both `:is()` and `:where()` simplify complex selector lists, but `:where()` always strips specificity to (0,0,0,0), making it ideal for easy CSS resets and base design systems.

questions.question: Which of the following CSS properties is inherited by child elements by default?
options: padding
background-color
border
font-family
questions.explanation: Typography and textual properties (like `color`, `font-family`, `font-size`, `line-height`, `letter-spacing`) inherit automatically, while box model properties (`margin`, `padding`, `border`, `background`) do not.

questions.question: What does setting a CSS property value to `initial` do?
options: It resets the property to the official W3C CSS specification default value, regardless of browser user-agent styles or parent inheritance
It forces the property to take the exact value computed by its immediate parent container
It makes the property inherit values from the `<body>` element only
It restores the value that was saved in the browser's local storage session
questions.explanation: The `initial` keyword sets a property to its default value as defined in the CSS specification (e.g., `color: initial` becomes `black`, `display: initial` becomes `inline`).

questions.question: How do you declare and access a CSS Custom Property (CSS variable) correctly?
options: Declare with `var:` prefix (e.g., `var:brand-blue: #0070f3;`) and access using `#brand-blue;`
Declare with `$` prefix (e.g., `$brand-blue: #0070f3;`) and access using `val($brand-blue);`
Declare with `--` prefix (e.g., `--brand-blue: #0070f3;`) and access using `var(--brand-blue, #000);`
Declare with `@` prefix (e.g., `@brand-blue: #0070f3;`) and access using `get(@brand-blue);`
questions.explanation: CSS variables are defined on any selector (often `:root`) with a `--` prefix and retrieved using the `var(--custom-property-name, fallback)` function.

questions.question: When two CSS rules have identical specificity and target the exact same element, how does the cascade determine which rule applies?
options: The rule that appears last in the stylesheet source order wins (Source Order rule)
The rule with the shorter property name is selected automatically
The browser randomly picks one rule during DOM construction
The rule declared in an external stylesheet always overrides internal styles regardless of order
questions.explanation: In the CSS Cascade algorithm, when origin, importance, and specificity are equal, the declaration appearing last in the stylesheet source order takes precedence.

questions.question: What is the primary performance drawback of using `@import` inside a CSS file compared to `<link rel="stylesheet">` in HTML?
options: `@import` disables all JavaScript execution on modern mobile web browsers
`@import` creates sequential waterfall network requests by waiting for the parent stylesheet to download before initiating child downloads
`@import` converts CSS colors to low-resolution monochrome gradients
`@import` files are completely ignored by search engine indexing bots
questions.explanation: `<link>` tags allow browsers to discover and download stylesheets in parallel, whereas `@import` delays stylesheet downloads by creating a blocking sequential network waterfall.

questions.question: What does the compound selector `.btn.primary` (without any space between classes) select?
options: Any element with class `primary` that is a descendant inside an element with class `btn`
Any HTML element that possesses both the `btn` class AND the `primary` class simultaneously
Only the first child element located inside the `.btn` container
Any element that has either the `btn` class OR the `primary` class
questions.explanation: Chaining classes without a space (`.btn.primary`) creates a compound selector matching elements that have both classes applied at the same time.

questions.question: Why should the `!important` declaration be avoided in general CSS authoring whenever possible?
options: It incurs monetary server hosting charges for each page render
It prevents browsers from caching CSS files in local storage
It causes browser rendering engines to crash when compiling CSSOM trees
It breaks the natural cascading specificity hierarchy and makes debugging and overriding styles difficult in larger codebases
questions.explanation: `!important` overrides normal specificity rules, creating maintenance headaches because the only way to override an `!important` declaration is another `!important` with higher specificity.

questions.question: Which pseudo-class targets an element when it receives focus specifically via keyboard navigation (such as Tab), while suppressing focus outlines on mouse clicks?
options: :focus
:hover
:active
:focus-visible
questions.explanation: `:focus-visible` applies focus indicators only when the user navigates via keyboard or assistive tech, avoiding unwanted focus rings during mouse clicks.

questions.question: What is the effect of the `:focus-within` pseudo-class?
options: It prevents all child elements within a form from receiving focus
It targets only the very first `<input>` inside an active modal dialog
It matches an element if the element itself OR any of its descendant children currently has keyboard/mouse focus
It matches an input field only when the user is actively typing text inside it
questions.explanation: `:focus-within` allows styling a parent container (like highlighting a whole form group or navigation bar) when any child element inside it gains focus.

questions.question: How does the pseudo-class `:not(.active)` behave on a selector `li:not(.active)`?
options: It hides all `<li>` elements that have the `.active` class using `display: none`
It selects all `<li>` elements that do NOT have the `.active` class applied
It selects only disabled button elements inside an inactive list
It removes the `.active` class from all `<li>` elements in the DOM
questions.explanation: The negation pseudo-class `:not(selector)` matches elements that do not match the selector list provided in its parenthesis.

questions.question: What does the `&` symbol represent in modern native CSS Nesting?
options: A command that forces the browser to recompile CSS into WebAssembly
A logical AND operator that requires two stylesheets to load simultaneously
An escape character used for unicode typography symbols
A nesting selector that explicitly references and represents the parent selector rule
questions.explanation: In modern native CSS nesting, `&` represents the parent selector, allowing modifier classes (e.g., `&.is-open`) and pseudo-classes (e.g., `&:hover`) to be nested cleanly.

questions.question: Which of the following styling approaches has the highest natural specificity according to the CSS cascade specification?
options: An external rule selecting multiple elements `header nav ul li a` (0,0,0,5)
An internal `<style>` tag rule combining three classes `.nav.menu.active` (0,0,3,0)
An external stylesheet rule with an ID selector `#main-header` (0,1,0,0)
Inline styles applied via HTML `style="..."` attribute (1,0,0,0)
questions.explanation: Inline styles have a specificity weight of (1,0,0,0), which naturally overrides any external or internal stylesheet selector unless `!important` is used.

lessons.lessonTitle: Lesson 2: The CSS Box Model: Margin, Padding, Border, & Content

questions.question: Under the standard default CSS box model (`box-sizing: content-box`), if an element has `width: 200px`, `padding: 20px`, `border: 5px solid black`, and `margin: 15px`, what is its total rendered horizontal space on the page?
options: 200px total occupied space
240px total occupied space
280px total occupied space (Content 200 + Padding Left/Right 40 + Border Left/Right 10 + Margin Left/Right 30)
250px total occupied space
questions.explanation: Under `content-box`, total horizontal space = Content (200px) + Padding (20px * 2 = 40px) + Border (5px * 2 = 10px) + Margin (15px * 2 = 30px) = 280px. Total element width is 250px.

questions.question: What is the primary advantage of setting `box-sizing: border-box` across all elements?
options: It eliminates the need for writing media queries on mobile viewport screens
It disables margin collapse across all nested block elements permanently
The specified `width` and `height` include content, padding, and border, making responsive sizing and layout math predictable
It automatically adds rounded corners and drop shadows to all HTML containers
questions.explanation: With `border-box`, setting `width: 300px` guarantees the element's outer border box is exactly 300px, absorbing padding and border inward rather than expanding outward.

questions.question: What is the standard CSS universal reset snippet used by modern developers to enforce consistent border-box sizing across all elements and pseudo-elements?
options: html { border-box: true; }
body { box-sizing: all; }
:root { sizing: border-box !default; }
*, *::before, *::after { box-sizing: border-box; }
questions.explanation: Targeting `*`, `*::before`, and `*::after` ensures every element and generated pseudo-element adheres to predictable `border-box` calculations.

questions.question: What occurs during 'Margin Collapse' between two adjacent vertical block-level elements?
options: The vertical margins merge into a single margin equal to the largest individual margin value, rather than adding together
The browser throws a CSS parsing warning and disables padding
The two elements are automatically forced onto the same horizontal line
The bottom element's margin is completely erased and set to 0px
questions.explanation: When adjacent block elements meet vertically, their top and bottom margins collapse into a single margin whose size equals the maximum of the two margins.

questions.question: Under what condition will `margin: 0 auto;` successfully center an element horizontally inside its parent container?
options: The element must have `display: inline` and no explicit width defined
The element must have `position: absolute` with `left: 0`
The element must be a block-level container with a specified, constrained `width` (or `max-width`) less than its parent
The parent container must have `overflow: scroll` enabled
questions.explanation: `margin: 0 auto` divides remaining horizontal space equally between left and right margins, which only works if the block element has an explicit width less than 100%.

questions.question: In the 4-value shorthand `margin: 10px 20px 30px 40px;`, which value corresponds to the left margin?
options: 10px (Top)
40px (Clockwise order: Top=10px, Right=20px, Bottom=30px, Left=40px)
20px (Right)
30px (Bottom)
questions.explanation: CSS 4-value box model shorthands follow a clockwise order: Top, Right, Bottom, Left (often remembered by the acronym TRouBLe).

questions.question: What is the key visual and layout difference between `outline` and `border` in CSS?
options: `outline` increases the total computed width of the element in the DOM
`outline` is only supported on SVG elements, whereas `border` is for HTML
`border` cannot have custom colors, whereas `outline` supports gradients
`outline` is drawn outside the element's border box and does NOT occupy space in the layout flow, so toggling it never causes content layout reflow
questions.explanation: Unlike `border`, an `outline` does not take up box model space or affect element dimensions, making it ideal for focus indicators without triggering layout shifts.

questions.question: What is the behavior of vertical margins (`margin-top` and `margin-bottom`) and vertical padding when applied to a pure inline element (like `<span>` or `<a>`)?
options: Vertical margins and padding push all preceding and succeeding text lines upward and downward identically to block elements
Vertical padding visual background renders but does NOT push surrounding line boxes away, and vertical margins have zero effect on layout spacing
Inline elements ignore all horizontal and vertical margins and padding completely
The browser automatically converts the inline element into `display: block`
questions.explanation: Inline elements only respect horizontal margins and padding for layout flow. Vertical padding will visually overlap adjacent lines without pushing them apart, and vertical margins are ignored.

questions.question: How does `display: inline-block` differ from `display: inline`?
options: `inline-block` allows setting explicit `width`, `height`, and respects top/bottom margins and padding while still sitting inline on the same line with adjacent content
`inline-block` forces the element onto its own brand new line like a `<div>`
`inline-block` is deprecated and behaves identically to `display: none`
`inline-block` disables all background colors and text decoration styling
questions.explanation: `inline-block` elements flow inline horizontally like text, but gain full box model capabilities (explicit `width`, `height`, `margin-top/bottom`, `padding-top/bottom`).

questions.question: What is the difference between `overflow: hidden` and `overflow: clip` in modern CSS?
options: `overflow: hidden` only works on images, whereas `overflow: clip` only works on text
`overflow: hidden` creates a scroll container (allowing programmatic scrolling via JS), whereas `overflow: clip` forbids all scrolling and reduces memory overhead
`overflow: clip` adds a visible scrollbar, while `overflow: hidden` hides the scrollbar
There is no difference; `clip` is just a legacy alias for `hidden`
questions.explanation: `overflow: hidden` prevents user scrolling while still allowing programmatic scrolling (creating a scroll container), whereas `overflow: clip` completely disables scrolling in all forms.

questions.question: What is the difference between `em` and `rem` units in CSS sizing?
options: `rem` is always relative to the root `<html>` font size, whereas `em` is relative to the immediate parent element's font size (which can compound with nesting)
`em` is relative to root font size, while `rem` is relative to viewport height
`rem` only applies to margins, while `em` only applies to font sizes
`em` is fixed to 16px forever, while `rem` changes based on device screen resolution
questions.explanation: `rem` (Root EM) scales consistently relative to the root `<html>` element (default 16px), preventing the nested compounding issue seen with `em` units.

questions.question: What does the CSS viewport unit `100dvh` represent compared to `100vh` on mobile web browsers?
options: `dvh` represents dual-screen display height on foldable smartphones
Dynamic Viewport Height (`dvh`) dynamically adjusts its size as mobile browser UI chrome (address bar and toolbars) expands or collapses during scrolling
`dvh` divides viewport height by device pixel ratio for desktop monitors only
`dvh` is static and ignores mobile browser address bars completely
questions.explanation: `dvh` (Dynamic Viewport Height) adapts in real time to mobile browser UI shifts (like address bar show/hide), resolving the dreaded 100vh overflow clipping bug on mobile.

questions.question: What is the effect of applying a negative margin, such as `margin-top: -20px;`, to an element?
options: It pulls the element 20px upward, overlapping any content situated above it in the layout flow
It collapses the height of the element to zero pixels
It creates 20px of transparent white empty space above the element
It rotates the element 180 degrees vertically
questions.explanation: Negative margins pull the element in the direction of the negative value (or pull subsequent siblings toward itself if applied to bottom/right), allowing deliberate overlapping layouts.

questions.question: What is the syntax order for the `box-shadow` property in CSS?
options: box-shadow: inset color offset-y offset-x spread-radius blur-radius;
box-shadow: color blur-radius spread-radius offset-x offset-y;
box-shadow: spread-radius blur-radius offset-y offset-x inset color;
box-shadow: offset-x offset-y blur-radius spread-radius color inset;
questions.explanation: Standard `box-shadow` syntax takes X-offset, Y-offset, optional blur radius, optional spread radius, color, and optional `inset` keyword.

questions.question: How do you create a perfect circle from a square element of `width: 100px; height: 100px;` using CSS?
options: clip-path: polygon(0 0, 100% 100%);
border-radius: 50%;
shape-outside: circle(100%);
border-radius: 100px 0 100px 0;
questions.explanation: Setting `border-radius: 50%` curves each corner by half the element's dimension, turning equal width and height squares into perfect circles.

questions.question: What does `width: fit-content;` do to an element's dimensions?
options: It forces the element to stretch across the entire screen regardless of parent width
It sets the width to exactly 0px until an image finishes loading
It sizes the element to shrink-wrap its content up to the available width, without stretching to 100% like a normal block
It resizes the font size until all text fits onto a single horizontal line
questions.explanation: `fit-content` allows an element to expand as needed to fit its contents, but caps its maximum width at the available space in its parent container.

questions.question: How does the CSS `clamp()` function work for responsive dimensions (e.g., `width: clamp(300px, 50vw, 800px);`)?
options: It sets a preferred value (`50vw`) that can scale dynamically, but guarantees the value will never drop below `300px` or exceed `800px`
It restricts the element's width to exactly 300px on mobile and 800px on tablet
It calculates the average of the three numbers and sets a fixed pixel width
It rotates through the three values at 1-second animation intervals
questions.explanation: `clamp(MIN, PREFERRED, MAX)` clamps a scalable value between an absolute minimum floor and maximum ceiling, eliminating messy media query breakpoints.

questions.question: What happens when an element with `width: 100%` is given `margin: 20px` inside a parent container under default `content-box`?
options: The margins are ignored completely because width is 100%
The parent container automatically expands to fit the margin without scrolling
The browser automatically reduces the width to 80% to compensate
The element overflows its parent container horizontally by 40px, causing unwanted horizontal scrollbars
questions.explanation: Under `content-box`, `100% width + 40px margin` exceeds the 100% boundary of the parent, spilling out and causing horizontal overflow.

questions.question: Which CSS mathematical function allows combining different measurement units in a single calculation (e.g., subtracting a fixed pixel sidebar from a percentage width)?
options: eval()
sum()
calc() (e.g., width: calc(100% - 250px);)
compute()
questions.explanation: The `calc()` function performs dynamic mathematical operations across mixed units, such as subtracting fixed pixel dimensions (`250px`) from relative percentages (`100%`).

questions.question: Why does vertical margin collapsing not occur between flex items or grid items?
options: Margin collapsing only works when using CSS tables
Browsers convert all margins to padding inside flex containers automatically
Flexbox and Grid items do not support any margin properties
The CSS Flexbox and Grid formatting contexts explicitly establish independent formatting roots that disable standard vertical block margin collapse
questions.explanation: Margins between flex items and grid items never collapse; their margins always stack additively because they operate in flex/grid formatting contexts rather than block formatting contexts.

lessons.lessonTitle: Lesson 3: CSS Colors, Typography, & Visual Backgrounds

questions.question: What is the key difference between setting opacity via `opacity: 0.5` versus setting a semi-transparent background via `background-color: rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.5)`?
options: `opacity: 0.5` only affects text color, leaving backgrounds fully opaque
`rgba()` disables all mouse click events on the element, while `opacity` does not
`opacity: 0.5` makes the target element AND all of its nested child elements semi-transparent, whereas `rgba()` only makes the background color semi-transparent
There is no difference; modern browsers treat them as identical rendering commands
questions.explanation: The `opacity` property affects the entire rendered stacking context including all child text and icons, whereas `rgba()` or `hsla()` only applies alpha transparency to the specific color property.

questions.question: What does the `currentcolor` keyword in CSS represent?
options: It queries the user's desktop wallpaper palette in modern browsers
It returns the default background color of the operating system window
It converts the closest hex color code into a web-safe RGB format
It references the computed value of the element's current `color` property, allowing borders, SVGs, or shadows to match text color dynamically
questions.explanation: `currentcolor` acts as a built-in CSS variable representing the value of the `color` property on that element (or inherited from its parent), commonly used in SVG fills and borders.

questions.question: Why is it considered a best practice to define a 'fallback font stack' (e.g., `font-family: 'Inter', Roboto, -apple-system, sans-serif;`)?
options: It allows the browser to download all four fonts simultaneously to increase rendering speed
If the user's browser fails to load or find the custom primary font, it gracefully falls back to available local system fonts rather than rendering broken characters
It is required by web hosting servers to validate font licensing certificates
It enables multiple languages to display simultaneously inside the same sentence
questions.explanation: A font stack provides an ordered fallback list; if the primary web font fails to load or is unavailable, the browser renders the next available system font.

questions.question: In the `@font-face` rule, what does setting `font-display: swap;` accomplish?
options: It displays a fallback system font immediately while the custom font downloads, then swaps in the custom font once loaded to prevent Invisible Text (FOIT)
It permanently disables custom web fonts on mobile data connections
It alternates between bold and italic fonts on every user click
It blocks the entire webpage rendering until the custom font is 100% downloaded
questions.explanation: `font-display: swap` prevents Flash of Invisible Text (FOIT) by rendering a fallback font immediately and swapping to the custom font once downloaded, improving perceived load performance.

questions.question: Why is setting a unitless `line-height` (e.g., `line-height: 1.5;`) strongly recommended over fixed pixel values (e.g., `line-height: 24px;`) on container elements?
options: Fixed pixel line-heights are completely ignored by modern mobile web browsers
Unitless line-height forces all paragraphs to take up exactly 100% of the viewport height
Unitless line-height converts all lowercase text to capital letters
Unitless `line-height` scales proportionally relative to each child element's individual `font-size`, preventing text collisions when children have larger headings
questions.explanation: When `line-height: 1.5` is inherited, child elements multiply 1.5 by their own font size. A fixed pixel value (e.g., `24px`) inherited by a `36px` heading causes text lines to overlap disastrously.

questions.question: What is the primary difference between `background-size: cover` and `background-size: contain`?
options: `contain` repeats the image 10 times, whereas `cover` only displays it once

`cover` scales the image to completely fill the container (cropping excess edges if aspect ratios differ), while `contain` scales the image so the entire image is visible without cropping (leaving letterboxing if needed)
`cover` compresses image file size, whereas `contain` keeps raw high-resolution data
`contain` only works with SVG vector graphics, while `cover` only works with PNGs
questions.explanation: `cover` guarantees no empty background space in the container by cropping edges as needed; `contain` guarantees the whole image is visible without cropping, potentially leaving uncovered space.

questions.question: Which CSS property creates a fixed 'Parallax' background effect where the background image stays stationary in the viewport while the rest of the page scrolls over it?
options: background-clip: viewport;
background-position: sticky;
background-attachment: fixed;
background-repeat: static;
questions.explanation: `background-attachment: fixed` fixes the background relative to the viewport, creating a classic parallax scrolling effect as content scrolls over the stationary image.

questions.question: Which combination of CSS properties is required to truncate a single line of overflowing text with an ellipsis (`...`)?
options: display: inline; line-clamp: 1; text-wrap: cut;
white-space: nowrap; overflow: hidden; text-overflow: ellipsis;
text-truncate: true; word-break: none;
overflow-wrap: break-word; text-overflow: clip;
questions.explanation: Single-line truncation requires preventing line breaks (`white-space: nowrap`), hiding overflow (`overflow: hidden`), and showing ellipsis (`text-overflow: ellipsis`) within a bounded width container.

questions.question: What CSS standard property controls whether the browser can break words across lines in order to prevent long words or URLs from overflowing its container?
options: hyphen-mode: auto;
overflow-wrap: break-word; (or word-break: break-all;)
text-wrap: force;
letter-spacing: compress;
questions.explanation: `overflow-wrap: break-word` (formerly `word-wrap`) allows unbroken strings like long URLs to break onto new lines when they would otherwise overflow their containing box.

questions.question: What is the numeric equivalent of the `font-weight: bold;` keyword in CSS?
questions.explanation: In the CSS numeric font-weight scale (100–900), `400` represents normal weight, `700` represents bold, and `900` represents black/extra bold.

questions.question: How are multiple background image layers stacked when defined in a single `background` property (e.g., `background: url(top.png), url(bottom.png);`)?
options: The browser blends all layers equally into a single 50% opacity composite
Only the largest file size image is displayed; the other is ignored
The first background image listed is rendered on top (closest to the user), with subsequent layers rendered underneath in descending order
The last background image listed is rendered on top
questions.explanation: Multiple backgrounds are layered from front to back: the first image listed in the comma-separated CSS rule appears on top, closest to the viewer.

questions.question: What is the syntax to create a smooth linear gradient transitioning from purple at the top to orange at the bottom?
options: background-image: gradient-linear(purple -> orange);
background-color: linear(from purple, to orange);
background: radial-direction(purple, orange, 180deg);
background-image: linear-gradient(to bottom, purple, orange);
questions.explanation: Linear gradients use the `linear-gradient(direction, color-stop-1, color-stop-2)` syntax, defaulting to `to bottom` (180deg) if direction is omitted.

questions.question: Which CSS property removes the default underline from hyperlinks (`<a>` tags)?
options: text-decoration: none;
text-underline: hidden;
font-decoration: remove;
link-style: plain;
questions.explanation: `text-decoration: none` removes typographic underlines, overlines, or line-through strokes from text elements.

questions.question: What is the modern CSS space-separated color syntax for an RGB color with 80% opacity?
options: color: rgb(34 197 94) opacity(0.8)
questions.explanation: Modern CSS Color Level 4 syntax allows space-separated RGB/HSL values with an optional slash `/` delimiter preceding alpha transparency (e.g., `rgb(r g b / alpha)`).

questions.question: What does the `text-transform: capitalize;` property do to text?
options: It capitalizes only the very first letter of the entire paragraph sentence
It converts the entire string into all capital uppercase letters
It converts the first letter of every individual word to uppercase while preserving the rest of the letters
It underlines all uppercase acronyms automatically
questions.explanation: `text-transform: capitalize` capitalizes the first character of each word, `uppercase` capitalizes every character, and `lowercase` makes all characters lowercase.

questions.question: What is the primary advantage of the OKLCH color space (`oklch(lightness chroma hue)`) over standard RGB/HSL in modern CSS?
options: It is perceptually uniform, meaning identical lightness values appear equally bright to human eyes across all different color hues
It converts all web pages into printable CMYK brochures automatically
It consumes 90% less GPU memory when rendering web animations
It is the only color format supported on iPhone mobile screens
questions.explanation: OKLCH solves HSL's perceptual distortion (where yellow at 50% lightness looks blindingly bright while blue at 50% looks dark) by maintaining true uniform perceptual lightness.

questions.question: How do you apply a multi-line text truncation to clamp a paragraph to exactly 3 visible lines with an ellipsis?
options: max-lines: 3; truncate: multi-line;
line-height: clamp(3); overflow: ellipsis;
display: -webkit-box; -webkit-line-clamp: 3; -webkit-box-orient: vertical; overflow: hidden;
text-lines: 3; text-overflow: ellipsis; overflow: clip;
questions.explanation: Multi-line clamping is achieved via WebKit box properties: `display: -webkit-box`, `-webkit-line-clamp: 3`, `-webkit-box-orient: vertical`, and `overflow: hidden`.

questions.question: What is the effect of `letter-spacing: 0.1em;` on a text heading?
options: It increases the blank space between words while keeping characters tight
It increases the vertical line spacing between rows of text
It sets the width of the font's bounding box to 0.1em
It increases the horizontal tracking space between individual characters by 0.1em
questions.explanation: `letter-spacing` adjusts tracking (the horizontal space between characters), while `word-spacing` adjusts the space between words.

questions.question: Which `background-clip` value allows text to take on the gradient color of the background image underneath it?
options: background-clip: text; (combined with color: transparent;)
background-clip: content-box;
background-clip: font-mask;
background-clip: border-box;
questions.explanation: `background-clip: text` (often `-webkit-background-clip: text`) clips the background graphic to the text character shapes, which when paired with `color: transparent` creates gradient text.

questions.question: What is the difference between `serif` and `sans-serif` generic font families?
options: `sans-serif` fonts cannot display bold or italic font weights

`serif` fonts have small decorative strokes or projections (serifs) at the ends of character strokes (like Times New Roman), while `sans-serif` fonts have clean, straight stroke ends (like Arial/Inter)
`serif` fonts are only used in computer terminal command prompts
`serif` fonts are exclusively designed for mobile touchscreen displays
questions.explanation: Serif typefaces feature small finishing projections/feet at line ends (traditional in print), whereas sans-serif (French for 'without serif') typefaces have clean modern geometric ends.
